Eating Disorders

weight · compensation · medical mimicsIs the weight low, and do binges carry compensation?

1Script2Urgent3Differential4Workup5Criteria6Severity7Treatment8Follow-upPractice
1Illness script
Bottom line
  • Weight sorts it: anorexia nervosa has a body mass index (BMI) under 18.5 with fear of weight gain; bulimia nervosa has normal weight or overweight with binges and compensatory behavior; binge eating disorder has binges without compensation
  • Exclude a medical cause first: in long-standing type 1 diabetes with early satiety and vomiting, order a gastric emptying study after endoscopy, before psychotherapy
  • Anorexia: nutritional rehabilitation and psychotherapy; bulimia: cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) plus fluoxetine; refeed gradually and watch phosphate
What it is

Disturbed eating driven by body shape and weight concerns (anorexia and bulimia nervosa), or loss-of-control binges without compensation (binge eating disorder)

Driver

Excessive concern with body shape and weight drives restriction or compensation

Associated

Depression commonly coexists with anorexia nervosa; binges are followed by guilt and low mood

Chain

Restriction loss of fat lowers leptin and gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) amenorrhea and low bone density

Vomiting hypokalemia, hypochloremia, metabolic alkalosis

Insights

Does purging rule out anorexia nervosa? No: the binge-eating/purging type of anorexia can also purge; weight separates it from bulimia CompensationSelf-induced vomiting is common in bulimia but not required: fasting, excessive exercise, laxatives, enemas, diuretics and diet pills also count

Is fear of eating in a diabetic patient with early satiety an eating disorder? Not until gastroparesis is excluded: fear of eating can follow the symptoms

2Urgent risks
Severe malnutritionAnorexia nervosa with BMI under 15, weight under 70% of ideal, unstable vital signs or cardiac dysfunction

If any of these is present, choose admit for nutritional rehabilitation.

RefeedingRapid feeding of a severely malnourished patient

If nutrition is restarted, choose increase calories gradually; watch phosphate, potassium and magnesium.

MnemonicCARBS (congestive heart failure, arrhythmias, rhabdomyolysis, bloating, seizures): the complications of refeeding
PurgingFrequent vomiting

If vomiting is frequent, choose check potassium and chloride: hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis is expected.

VomitingMallory-Weiss tears are usually seen with alcohol use disorder or bulimia nervosa
3Differential
Look-alikes, most tempting first
DiagnosisFingerprintDurationDecides it
Bulimia nervosaLoss-of-control binges, then vomiting, fasting, exercise or laxatives; shape and weight concernsAt least weekly for 3 monthsNormal weight or overweight; vomiting not required
Anorexia nervosa, binge-eating/purging typeBinges and purging with intense fear of weight gainBMI under 18.5
Binge eating disorderRecurrent loss-of-control binges; obesity and type 2 diabetes riskNo compensatory behavior
Anorexia nervosa, restricting typeRestriction, fear of weight gain, distorted body image; amenorrhea, lanugo, bradycardia AssociatedHypercarotenemia, mitral valve prolapse, anemia, low bone density with stress fracturesBMI under 18.5 without binges
Gastroparesis (medical mimic)Long-standing type 1 diabetes; early satiety, postprandial vomiting, weight loss; worried by the weight loss CausesMost often idiopathic; also diabetes (type 1 more than type 2), medications such as tricyclics and calcium channel blockers, and surgeryLong-standing diabetesDelayed emptying on a gastric emptying study, after endoscopy excludes obstruction
Avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID)Avoids foods for their sensory features or the experience of eatingTypically begins in infancy or early childhoodNo body-image disturbance
Body dysmorphic disorderPreoccupation with a perceived defect in appearanceNot diagnosed when weight concern meets eating disorder criteria
Primary adrenal insufficiencyMay cause vomiting, weight loss and decreased appetite, without fear of eatingDecreased appetite without fear of eating; an adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) stimulation test can help diagnose it
4Workup
Clues that change the answer
CluePoints toNext move
Dorsal hand calluses, parotid enlargement, enamel erosion at normal weightBulimia nervosa with vomitingCBT, nutritional rehabilitation and fluoxetine
Lanugo, amenorrhea, bradycardia, yellow-tinged skinAnorexia nervosaNutritional rehabilitation and psychotherapy; hospitalize for BMI under 15, unstable vital signs or cardiac dysfunction
Binges without compensation, obesityBinge eating disorderCBT or behavioral weight loss therapy; a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI), lisdexamfetamine or topiramate
Type 1 diabetes with early satiety, vomiting and worry about weight lossGastroparesisEndoscopy, then a gastric emptying study
Low urine chloride with metabolic alkalosisCovert vomitingTreat as bulimia or binge-eating/purging anorexia, by weight

Pause point. The bait: CBT or an SSRI for a diabetic patient whose stress about eating follows early satiety and vomiting, where an eating disorder is less likely. Psychiatric diagnoses come after medical causes are excluded.

5Diagnostic criteria
Anorexia BMI – under 18.5 · Fear – intense fear of weight gain · Body image – distorted view of weight and shape · Types – restricting or binge-eating/purging
Bulimia Episodes – binges with compensatory behavior · Frequency – at least weekly for 3 months · Self-view – driven by shape and weight · Weight – normal or overweight
Binge eating Episodes – recurrent loss-of-control binges · Compensation – none
ARFID Avoidance – sensory features of food · Onset – typically infancy or early childhood · Body image – not disturbed

Where to treat
FindingAction

Olanzapine LimitsOlanzapine is used for weight gain, with limited evidence and known adverse effects; SSRIs treat comorbid anxiety or depression, not anorexia itself
3

Bulimiabulimia nervosa

CBT and nutritional rehabilitation plus fluoxetine ; not bupropion: it can cause seizures in bulimia
4

Binge eatingbinge eating disorder

CBT or behavioral weight loss therapy; an SSRI, lisdexamfetamine or topiramate
5

Small, low-fat meals; a prokinetic such as metoclopramide or erythromycin may be added
8Follow-up
Follow-up decisions
WhenDo
Refeeding beginsFollow the refeeding plan in step 2 (Urgent risks)
Long-standing anorexiaExpect low bone density and stress fractures; the bone loss is typically not reversible
Depression coexistsTreat the depression; an SSRI may be used for it
Practice
  1. 24-year-old woman eats large amounts rapidly several times a week and cannot stop Afterward she fasts for a day and runs extra miles; she hates her body shape BMI 21; pulse 98; she denies vomiting → Bulimia nervosa → Binges with compensatory fasting and exercise at a normal weight are bulimia nervosa; vomiting is not required, and binge-purge anorexia needs a BMI under 18.5
  2. 25-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes since childhood has lost 6 kg in 4 months She feels full after a few bites, vomits after meals, and worries about losing weight Upper endoscopy was normal; electrolytes and thyroid function normal → Gastric emptying study → Long-standing type 1 diabetes with early satiety and postprandial vomiting suggests gastroparesis; with obstruction excluded, a gastric emptying study confirms it before any psychiatric diagnosis
  3. 22-year-old runner has missed her periods for 5 months She eats one small meal a day, fears gaining weight and thinks her thighs are large BMI 16.8; pulse 48; fine hair on her back; no binges → Anorexia nervosa → Restriction with fear of weight gain, a distorted body image and a BMI under 18.5, plus amenorrhea, bradycardia and lanugo, is anorexia nervosa
  4. 23-year-old woman with anorexia nervosa comes for a scheduled visit She has lost more weight and feels dizzy whenever she stands BMI 14.5; pulse 38/min; blood pressure 82/50 mm Hg → Hospital admission for nutritional rehabilitation → A BMI under 15 with unstable vital signs is an indication for hospitalization, where nutritional rehabilitation begins
  5. 26-year-old woman with severe anorexia nervosa is admitted to the hospital A high-calorie feeding plan is started on the first day By day 3 she has weakness, palpitations and new leg swelling → Hypophosphatemia → Rapid refeeding triggers an insulin surge that lowers phosphate, potassium and magnesium; heart failure and arrhythmias can follow, so calories are increased gradually
  6. 20-year-old woman with bulimia nervosa purges several times a week She has low mood and asks for a medication that could also help her quit smoking Exam shows parotid swelling and calluses on the backs of her hands → Fluoxetine with CBT → Bulimia nervosa is treated with CBT, nutritional rehabilitation and fluoxetine; bupropion is avoided because it can cause seizures in these patients
  7. 38-year-old man with obesity eats large meals in secret several nights a week He feels out of control and ashamed but never vomits, fasts or overexercises BMI 34; hemoglobin A1c is elevated → Binge eating disorder → Recurrent loss-of-control binges without compensatory behavior are binge eating disorder, which raises the risk of obesity and type 2 diabetes
Pairs with Major Depressive Disorder: depression that coexists with an eating disorder. SSRI Adverse Effects: fluoxetine, and why not bupropion.
Transferable rule

Exclude a medical cause of early satiety and vomiting, then sort by weight and by whether binges carry compensation.
